cards.heading: Definition
cards.question: What are the four golden signals, and what rule of thumb governs them?
cards.answer: Latency, traffic, errors and saturation — the minimal measurement set held to give adequate monitoring coverage of a user-facing service; if you can measure only four things about a system, measure these.

cards.heading: Why latency is split by outcome
cards.question: Why must latency be measured separately for successful and failed requests rather than as one mean?
cards.answer: An instant error (e.g. a dropped backend connection) pulls the mean latency down and hides the failure. A slow error is worse than a fast one, so error latency is tracked separately rather than filtered out.

cards.heading: Three kinds of errors
cards.question: What three kinds of failure does the errors signal need to count, beyond explicit failures like a 500?
cards.answer: Explicit (a 500), implicit (a 200 carrying the wrong content, caught only by end-to-end tests), and by policy (any request slower than a committed response-time budget).

cards.heading: Saturation target and leading indicator
cards.question: Why is saturation's utilization target set below 100%, and what is often its earliest indicator?
cards.answer: Most systems degrade before they saturate, so the target sits below full utilization; rising 99th-percentile latency over a short window is often the earliest indicator of approaching saturation.

cards.heading: Scope of the claim
cards.question: What does the four golden signals framework claim about a service that measures and pages on all four?
cards.answer: Only that it is 'at least decently covered' — a reachable floor for monitoring, not a complete description of the system.
